'''''Iris pseudacorus''''', the '''yellow flag''', '''yellow iris''', or '''water flag''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Iridaceae]].  It is [[native plant|native]] to Europe, western Asia and northwest Africa. Its [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] ''pseudacorus'' means "false acorus", referring to the similarity of its leaves to those of ''[[Acorus calamus]]'' (sweet flag), as they have a prominently veined mid-rib and sword-like shape. However, the two plants are not closely related.

==Description==
This [[herbaceous]] flowering [[perennial plant]] grows to {{convert|100|-|150|cm|abbr=on}}, or a rare {{convert|2|m|abbr=on}} tall, with erect leaves up to {{convert|90|cm|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|3|cm|abbr=on}} broad. The flowers are bright yellow, {{convert|7|-|10|cm|abbr=on}} across, with the typical iris form. The fruit is a dry [[capsule (fruit)|capsule]] {{convert|4|-|7|cm|abbr=on}} long, containing numerous pale brown seeds.

''I. pseudacorus'' grows best in very wet conditions, and is common in wetlands, where it tolerates submersion, low [[pH]], and [[Anoxic waters|anoxic]] soils. The plant spreads quickly, by both [[rhizome]] and water-dispersed seed. It fills a similar [[ecological niche|niche]] to that of ''[[Typha]]'' and often grows with it, though usually in shallower water. While it is primarily an aquatic or marginal plant, the rhizomes can survive prolonged dry conditions.

Large ''I. pseudacorus'' stands in western Scotland form a very important feeding and breeding habitat for the endangered [[corncrake]].

''I. pseudacorus'' is one of two iris species native to the United Kingdom, the other being ''[[Iris foetidissima]]'' (stinking iris).

==Nectar production==
The plant was rated in second place for per day nectar production per flower in a [[UK]] plants survey conducted by the AgriLand project, which is supported by the UK Insect Pollinators Initiative. However, when number of flowers per floral unit, flower abundance, and [[phenology]] were taken into account, it dropped out of the top 10 for most nectar per unit cover per year, as did all plants that placed in the top ten, with the exception of common comfrey, ''[[Symphytum officinale]]''.<ref name=Pollinators>{{cite web |title=Which flowers are the best source of nectar? |publisher=Conservation Grade |url=http://www.conservationgrade.org/2014/10/which_flowers_best_source_nectar/ |access-date=2017-10-18 |date=2014-10-15 |archive-date=2019-12-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191214024659/http://www.conservationgrade.org/2014/10/which_flowers_best_source_nectar/ }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
It is widely planted in [[temperateness|temperate]] regions as an ornamental plant,<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Iris pseudacorus''|url=http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=3237|archive-url=https://archive.today/20121224083145/http://apps.rhs.org.uk/plantselector/plant?plantid=3237|archive-date=December 24, 2012|access-date=24 June 2013}}</ref> with several [[cultivar]]s selected for [[bog garden]] planting. The following cultivars have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]:<ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 53 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 13 March 2018}}</ref> 
* 'Roy Davidson'<ref>{{cite web | url =https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/110748/Iris-pseudacorus-Roy-Davidson/Details | title = Roy Davidson | publisher = RHS | access-date = 25 September 2020}}</ref> 
*'Variegata'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Iris pseudacorus'' 'Variegata'|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/98016/Iris-pseudacorus-Variegata-(v)/Details | access-date = 7 September 2020}}</ref> (it has leaves that are edged with deep white stripes<ref name="Cuttle">{{cite book |last1=Spencer-Jones |first1=Rae |last2=Cuttle |first2=Sarah |title=Wild Flowers of Britain and Ireland |date=2005 |publisher=Kyle Cathie Limited |location=London |isbn=978-1-85626-503-4 |page=88}}</ref>)

Other cultivars known include ''Alba'' (with pale cream flowers) and ''Golden Fleece'' (with dark yellow flowers).<ref name="Cuttle"/>

==Invasive species==
[[File:Yellow Iris, N Lagoon Dr, Vancouver, BC, CA imported from iNaturalist photo 509998191.jpg|thumb|Introduced, in [[British Columbia]]]]
In some regions (including the US and [[South Africa]])<ref name="Rhodes-CBC-2019-AR">{{cite web | url=http://www.ru.ac.za/media/rhodesuniversity/content/zoologyandentomology/cbc/informationdocuments/CBC_2019_Annual_Report.pdf | title=Centre for Biological Control Annual Report 2019 | editor1-first=Esther | editor1-last=Mostert | editor2-first=Kim | editor2-last=Weaver | publisher=[[Centre for Biological Control]], Rhodes University}}</ref> where it is not native, it has escaped from cultivation to establish itself as an [[invasive species|invasive]] [[aquatic plant]] which can create dense, monotypic stands, outcompeting other plants in the ecosystem. Where it is invasive, it is tough to remove on a large scale. Even ploughing the rhizomes is often ineffective. It has been banned in some areas but is still widely sold in others for use in gardens.<ref name=Spruce>{{cite news |last1=McIntosh |first1=Jamie |title=9 Top Types of Iris for the Flower Garden |url=https://www.thespruce.com/irises-for-flower-garden-1315808 |access-date=29 July 2021 |work=The Spruce |date=21 June 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

''Iris pseudacorus'' is reported as invasive in [[Connecticut]], [[Delaware]], [[Maryland]], [[New Hampshire]], [[New Jersey]], [[North Carolina]], [[Oregon]], [[Tennessee]], [[Virginia]], [[Vermont]], [[Washington (state)|Washington]], [[Wisconsin]], and [[West Virginia]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Laboratory |first=NOAA Great Lakes Environmental Research |title=NOAA National Center for Research on Aquatic Invasive Species (NCRAIS) |url=https://nas.er.usgs.gov/queries/greatlakes/FactSheet.aspx?Species_ID=1115 |access-date=2022-06-14 |website=nas.er.usgs.gov}}</ref>

==Relationship to ''fleur-de-lis''==
According to [[Pierre Augustin Boissier de Sauvages]], an 18th-century French [[Natural history|naturalist]] and [[lexicography|lexicographer]], the name ''[[fleur-de-lis]]'' applied to the [[Heraldry|heraldic]] symbol may be related to ''Iris pseudacorus'' rather than to a lily, based on the shape and yellow colour of the flower.<ref name= "Sauvages1756">{{cite book| author= Pierre Augustin Boissier de Sauvages |title=Languedocien Dictionnaire François|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=B8RDAAAAcAAJ&pg=PA154| access-date=27 July 2013|year=1756|pages=153–154 |language=fr}}</ref>

==Toxicity and uses==
The plant's roots and leaves are toxic.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|page=261|oclc=244766414|orig-date=1982}}</ref>

This plant has been used as a form of water treatment since it can take up macronutrients (such as [[nitrogen]] and [[phosphorus]]) through its roots,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mohseni-Bandpei |first1=A. |title=Nitrogen and phosphorus removal from wastewater by subsurface wetlands planted with Iris pseudacorus |journal=Ecological Engineering |date=2010 |volume=36 |issue=6 |pages=777–782|doi=10.1016/j.ecoleng.2010.02.002 |bibcode=2010EcEng..36..777Y }}</ref> and is featured in many AS Level Biology practicals as its ability to grow in low pH levels makes it a useful indicator.{{citation needed|date=September 2020}}

It can also [[Halophyte|withstand high salinity levels]] in the water.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zhao |first1=Huilin |last2=Wang |first2=Fen |last3=Ji |first3=Min |title=Brackish Eutrophic Water Treatment by Iris pseudacorus L.-Planted Microcosms: Physiological Responses of Iris pseudacorus L. to Salinity |journal=International Journal of Phytoremediation |date=2015 |volume=17 |issue=9 |pages=814–821 |doi=10.1080/15226514.2014.981240|pmid=25529785 |bibcode=2015IJPhy..17..814Z |s2cid=30542002 }}</ref>
